title: Make the agent reuse the existing empty-state component, not a one-off dashed box
summary:
The PR handles "no items" with a dashed border, a generic "Nothing here," and a one-off button. The repo already has an EmptyState (or BlankSlate) component with a slot for an icon, a title, a short description, and the primary action. Nearby lists use it. The new box uses different spacing, a different heading level, and a CTA that does not match the existing empty-state tone.

I've started treating a homemade empty box as a missed component, not as a lighter placeholder. The dashed border is easy to sketch. Shared typography and action placement are why the component exists.

Why the one-off empty box shows up

title: Optimized Prompting for Modern Reasoning LLMs
summary:
TL;DR: Many traditional prompting methods over-instruct and hinder modern reasoning LLMs. This guide explains how to use optimized prompting to get faster, more accurate results by leveraging the model's internal thought process.

Many developers still rely on rigid, overly specific prompts that were more effective with older, less capable LLMs. This approach often leads to verbose, slow, and sometimes inaccurate responses from advanced models like Claude 3 Opus or Gemini 1.5 Pro. These modern LLMs possess sophisticated reasoning capabilities that are underutilized when they are simply told what to do at every step. It’s like giving a senior developer a list of junior-level tasks to execute without letting them decide the optimal approach.

title: Workflow is 10x faster, again
summary:

title: How FIPS led to leaner container images for everyone
summary:
It started with a familiar story. A Trivy scan of our service image flagged six distinct critical vulnerabilities and nine distinct high-severity vulnerabilities across curl and libcurl. We expected to rush out a patch. Then we traced what curl was doing in the image. Its only job was to make a health check request to localhost. Did we need it there at all?

That question took on more urgency as we worked with teams running self-hosted Pulumi Cloud in air-gapped networks or inside FedRAMP authorization boundaries. When those teams run our images inside their own networks, every package in them becomes theirs to scan, justify in a security review, and keep patched. Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO. title: I built 59 free browser-based dev tools in vanilla JS — here's what I learned
summary:
I've been quietly building Antigravity Tools — a collection of 59 free, browser-based developer utilities — and today I'm sharing everything I built and learned.

Why vanilla JS? No React, no build step.

The main constraint I set for myself: zero dependencies, zero server, zero telemetry.

When you paste your JWT token into jwt.io, it goes to their server. When you use an online regex tester, your test strings are logged. I built Antigravity Tools so every operation runs inside your browser, using native APIs.

No Node.js backend
No npm packages
No webpack/vite/parcel
No Google Analytics
No cookies
